provenance: Observable checks adapted from the training taxonomy physical constraints and public optics knowledge; no benchmark sample prompts, questions, answers, or scores. Specific conditional image laws checked against cited author/publisher, university and weather-service references. Reference URLs are audit metadata, not sent to the judge.

rules.text: Intensity or color patterns remain within the identified transparent stressed or anisotropic material.
Pattern appearance is compatible with the requested polarization and viewing arrangement; ordinary tint or reflection is not sufficient evidence.
Spatial variations respect the material boundaries and geometry; no universal straight or smooth stripe pattern is required.
Concentrated bright curves, patches or networks appear on an identifiable receiving surface, not only as a surface glint.
The light-shaping water, glass or curved reflector and receiving region have a plausible visible relationship.
Light concentration follows the shaping surface and receiver; arbitrary luminous painted patterns are not evidence.
The compact ring or glow is centered on the viewed Sun, Moon or lamp, rather than an observer shadow.
Ring appearance is compatible with the requested droplet-layer context and source position.
The visible feature is distinguishable from lens ghosts, a large ice halo or an antisolar glory.
Image content belongs to the visible curved reflective surface and corresponds to an identifiable source object or environment.

For a real object in a convex spherical mirror, the image is upright and reduced; a concave mirror with the object inside its focal length gives an upright enlarged image, while a resolved real image is inverted. Judge scale only with adequate perspective references.
Occlusion, mirror boundaries and reflected views remain consistent with one camera viewpoint.
Spikes originate at compact bright source images, rather than appearing as detached physical light beams.
Spike arrangement is compatible with the specified aperture or obstruction where this is observable; do not infer an exact blade count without evidence.
The effect remains an imaging artifact, distinguishable from volumetric shafts and displaced lens ghosts.
Separated colors or wavelength-dependent deflection follow the specified transparent dispersive element.

For ordinary glass under white light and normal dispersion, the exiting violet ray is deflected more from the incident direction than the red ray; evaluate only if paths and interfaces are identifiable, not by arbitrary screen-left/right ordering.
The effect is distinguishable from painted color, grating orders and colored illumination.
The intended focal subject and visible depth relationships support a coherent sharpness distribution.
Defocused regions show plausible blur or bokeh rather than a global motion smear or fog substitute.
Transitions and object boundaries remain compatible with the requested lens/focus arrangement; not every depth plane must be sharp.
Reference lines or spatial structures visibly show the requested lens mapping.
Curvature or stretching follows a coherent image mapping rather than arbitrary local object deformation.
Perspective convergence and naturally curved objects are not treated as proof of lens distortion.
Spectra, diffraction orders or spot patterns are associated with the identified periodic optical surface.
Visible order orientation, spacing and colors are compatible with the requested source and grating geometry where assessable.
Colors are not a uniform painted rainbow or a prism/thin-film substitute; limited visible orders are allowed.
The requested disk deformation or color-rim feature occurs on the low-altitude celestial disk.
Visible disk structure is compatible with the horizon and atmospheric layering, rather than an unrelated lens ghost.
An ordinary orange disk alone does not demonstrate the requested refractive effect; duration is not inferred from a still image.
The ring or arc is geometrically related to the Sun or Moon, with a plausible ice-halo appearance.
Visible geometry and color ordering are consistent with the requested halo subtype where evidence permits.
Cloud gaps and partial field of view can interrupt the halo; a complete uniformly bright circle is not mandatory.

internal_reflection.name: Total internal reflection and Snell windows

rules.text: For total internal reflection, light reaches the interface from higher to lower refractive index above the critical angle; when paths are observable there is reflected light inside, not a propagating transmitted ray into the lower-index medium.
For underwater Snell-window scenes, the transmitted above-water view and reflected underwater regions remain distinguishable.
Guided/reflected paths or interface views are compatible with the stated geometry; a circular frame or ordinary air-side water reflection alone is insufficient.
Ghosts, stray patches or veiling glare are compatible with the strong-light direction relative to the camera.
Artifacts behave as image-plane lens effects rather than extra physical objects or emitted scene beams.
Their appearance is distinguishable from scene reflections, bokeh or diffraction spikes alone.
Objects seen through the lens correspond coherently to the surrounding real scene.

For a real object, a diverging thin lens gives an upright reduced virtual image; a converging magnifier used inside its focal length gives an upright enlarged virtual image. Check scale only with adequate references, not equal screen-pixel distances.
Lens boundary transitions and occlusions are coherent; a projected real image is not substituted for the requested virtual view.
Apparent vertical bands are visibly associated with the appropriate light sources and ice-crystal environment.
Pillar placement is compatible with reflection geometry rather than literal upward emitted laser columns.
Ordinary beams, aurora, sensor streaks or water reflections do not replace the requested atmospheric effect.

long_exposure.name: Long exposure, motion blur and flash trails

rules.text: Motion trails or blur follow a plausible continuous exposure and the requested relative camera/subject motion.
Stationary references and tracked subjects have a coherent sharpness relationship; stationary objects need not blur.
When flash trails are requested, frozen detail and ambient trails are mutually consistent rather than pasted repeated subjects.
Droplet-filled cloud or fog visibly interacts with illumination through glow, attenuation or scattering.
Depth-dependent visibility and contrast are compatible with the atmospheric path and scene lighting.
Defocus, white painted objects or arbitrary image blur do not replace the requested scattering phenomenon.
The distant reference scene has the requested displaced, inverted or layered apparent image structure.
The altered image is associated with a plausible atmospheric layer or near-horizon region.
Water reflections, ordinary haze and random heat shimmer are not substituted for the requested layered mirage.
Successive reflected objects correspond consistently to the real objects and participating mirror surfaces.
Repeated views, orientations and occlusions are compatible with the visible mirror arrangement.
Image counts respect field of view and occlusion; no universal image-count formula is imposed without the required geometry.
The transparent-media boundary and a corresponding object or background make the refracted view identifiable.

For an air-side near-normal view through a flat water surface, submerged detail appears shallower when depth references permit checking; visible rays bend toward the normal entering a higher-index medium and away leaving it. Curved vessels need their own geometry.
Corresponding object portions remain coherent across the interface; no universal inversion or magnification is imposed on all vessels.
The cloud or mist phenomenon is associated with the antisolar direction, consistent with illumination behind the observer.
If glory rings are requested, rings occur about the observer-related center; an ordinary shadow alone is insufficient.
For a shadow-only Brocken request, the shadow lies on mist/cloud and is not incorrectly required to include colored rings.
The requested bright patch or arc has a plausible relation to the Sun and requested oriented-ice-crystal subtype.
Visible arc curvature, location and colors are compatible with the subtype where the reference geometry is adequate.
Paired patches and equal brightness are not universally required; arbitrary colored clouds are insufficient evidence.
The illuminated path is visibly present within an identifiable particle or colloidal medium.
Path visibility and medium boundaries are compatible with the stated source and suspension geometry.
Surface glints or visible apparatus without an illuminated scattering path do not satisfy the requested effect.
Reflected objects, identities and visible poses correspond coherently to the actual scene.
Mirror field of view, boundaries and occlusion are consistent with one camera viewpoint and mirror plane.

For an ordinary plane mirror the virtual image is upright, with unchanged physical size and equal perpendicular object/image distances from the plane; apply only where scene references support it, never demand equal image-pixel sizes or naive screen-left/right reversal.
A plausible primary bow is visible in a rain or spray region with compatible source-observer geometry.
When spectral bands are resolved, the primary bow has red on its outer edge and blue/violet on its inner edge; do not require all colors in a faint or red sunset bow.
Arc extent follows available droplets and field of view; partial bows and circular elevated views are allowed.
Sky color or aerial perspective is tied to atmospheric illumination or visible scene distance.
Color and contrast vary plausibly with atmospheric path and lighting context.
Blue pigment, arbitrary color grading and shallow-focus blur do not substitute for atmospheric scattering.
The visible rainbow subtype matches the requested mechanism: reflected illumination, a water-mirrored bow, or higher-order droplet scattering.
Bow position and orientation are compatible with the source, water plane when relevant, and droplet region.
A generic reflected primary bow is not evidence of a higher-order bow; color/arc geometry must support the requested subtype when visible.
Bright return is localized to a plausible passive retroreflective material under near-observer illumination.
Material extent and visible brightness are coherent with the source/view relationship.
Self-emitting lamps, plain bright paint and unrelated specular highlights do not substitute for retroreflection.
The requested secondary bow or double-bow structure is present in the appropriate droplet region.
When both bows and colors are resolved, the secondary lies outside the primary around the same antisolar center, with red on its inner edge and blue/violet on its outer edge.
The interbow region and relative visibility are plausible; fine supernumerary fringes or water reflections do not replace a secondary bow.

shadow_source.name: Single-source shadows and natural aperture projections

rules.text: Where source and receiver cues establish direction, an opaque object blocks light on the receiver behind it along incoming light paths; same-plane sun shadows share one directional illumination, allowing perspective convergence.

For a resolved extended-source shadow, partially illuminated penumbra is lighter than fully blocked umbra when present; shadow softness must fit source angular extent and object-receiver separation. Do not demand a visible umbra in every geometry.
For solar aperture projection, bright patches reproduce the resolved solar disk rather than necessarily the aperture shape; during a partial eclipse they show the appropriate obscured disk.

For repeated eclipse aperture projections on the same plane under the same illumination, the resolved solar silhouettes have consistent obscuration orientation, allowing perspective and aperture blur.
Transmitted or attenuated light is visibly related to the transparent/translucent object and receiver.
Color, silhouette and diffusion are plausible for the stated material and illumination.
Passive material is not treated as an independent emitter, and colored multi-source shadows or caustic patterns do not replace transmission.
The requested subtype is visible: fine supernumerary fringes or a broad weakly colored fogbow.
The feature is related coherently to the rainbow direction, droplet region and source-observer arrangement.
A secondary bow, reflection bow or compact glory does not substitute for the requested subtype.
Color appearance is localized to the plausible biological/material microstructure and respects its boundaries.
Spatial angle-dependent or reflective color is compatible with the material and ordinary illumination.
Paint or luminous overlays do not replace the structure; temporal color change cannot be established from one still image.
The reflected scene or highlight is associated with an identifiable reflecting surface.
Reflection placement, roughness-dependent spread and distortion are coherent with the surface and viewpoint.
Transmitted underwater content, focused caustics and unrelated bright patches do not replace the requested surface reflection.
Interference color or intensity patterns are localized to the identified thin-film region.
Pattern variations are compatible with the film geometry, thickness variation and illumination where observable.
Printed rainbows, colored lamps and unrelated reflected scenery do not substitute for film interference.
Local deformation or degradation is visible against reference edges or spatial detail through the affected air path.
Distortion is compatible with the thermal/exhaust context rather than uniform lens mapping or simple defocus.
A single image is not claimed to prove temporal flicker; stable layered mirages are distinguished from irregular turbulence.
Light shafts or volume shadows are visibly supported by scattering air or water.
Their position and occlusion are coherent with the source and gaps/obstacles.
Perspective convergence is compatible with viewing geometry; surface-only patches or lens spikes do not substitute for volume illumination.

Normal optical dispersion for common transparent media.
